before: For those from circumcision despise him, because with unforgetting memory he keeps the ordinances of God (Psalm 118:162 [119:162]).

The saying also has David’s own particular meaning: when he was pursued by Saul without cause and out of envy, his fear of God restrained him from taking vengeance. But it extends also to the common case, that there is no other way to escape wars of princes unharmed unless one is guarded by the fear of God.
After the gift of wisdom he asks again for salvation from dangers. This too is a reward for his willing zeal for the divine law (Psalm 118:173 [119:173]) (Ps 118:174-175).

So then he was truly saying just now that he awaited eternal salvation, and now also, longing for it, he has made this the goal of his study of the law. For he says that he will live again and praise God, helped toward this by his all-wise judgments (Ps 119:2). This is Christ, who comes down in place of human beings to the saving death for human beings, and by his suffering redeems those in sufferings, and by his death redeems the dying. And in accordance with this there follows, “My soul will live,” and what comes after (Psalm 118:175 [119:175]).

This was so immediately after the first apostasy of the human being, when Cain by deceit struck down his brother, and it is so throughout the whole present age, as is shown in other cases and in the present matter. So the person who looks to God, worn down and afflicted by this, asks for salvation from him. He does not foresee the cessation that will come then, when he is brought up to dwell in the peaceful city, with good and bad alike sharing its citizenship (Ps 119:5).

Another passage also indicates the foreign land in one respect, into which Israel fell and sojourned, and that his sojourning was extended to the greatest length. Prophesying in lament he brings this out so that it reaches also to the present condition; for this is the longest sojourning (Ps 119:7).

For the good and godly keep peace as far as depends on them and with all human beings, whenever there is no need of judicial punishment such as God commanded against the Canaanites and Amorites, forbidding friendship with them (Ps 120:1b). But the wicked and those who do not know God would never enter into friendship with the good; rather they abhor godliness, and they do not receive kindly anything good from the godly, nor are they tamed by their kindness.
He calls mountains here the invisible and heavenly powers. And while he awaits help through them, he says that the help does not originate from them but from the Creator (Psalm 120:1b-2 [121:1b-2]).

It is a joy to hear what is said by the angels, clearly the ones who speak to the prophets and who, as it were, lead the herd of Israel. Such is the one made known through Zechariah, interceding for fallen Jerusalem and speaking of her future dwelling (Ps 121:1b). The psalmist says that he rejoiced when he heard these things, and that he foresaw the secure dwelling in the holy city and, as it were, perceived the matter as present prophetically. For this is what “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem” means (Psalm 121:1b-4 [122:1b-4]) (Ps 122:2). The standing of feet is the immovable dwelling which the holy prophets also proclaim. The opposite of this was when, according to the history, God shook the foot of Jerusalem from its own land. So the psalmist speaks of the rebuilding of the city, seen by him as also by Ezekiel, and says that the building is of a city united—not, clearly, in the customary way of walls uniting it, but of the inhabitants united to one another. Therefore he did not say “city” but “as a city” having its joining together at once. For neither Ezekiel nor Zechariah declares that it will be inhabited under walls, but unwalled, and that its wall will be the Lord, since God is the guardian and holder together of the unity of the saints. He interprets the unity as being through the inhabitants themselves, saying, “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps 122:4). Not because walls were thrown around them were they united, but because they themselves were united through themselves. It is a testimony to Israel, clearly witnessing to the truth of the promises, and to give thanks to the name of the Lord, because confession of grace is owed by the beneficiaries to the one who fulfilled the wonderful promise.

before: He says that thrones of the house of David were established in her, since Daniel also prophesies a kingdom over all things. It is not the rule of some one person or of a single ruler, but a common kingdom for the best and most godly, through whom the kingdom of David is set upright by the grace of Christ, who gave to the twelve apostles the right to sit on twelve thrones and judge Israel.

But he will not allow good subjects to be corrupted by evil demons. Rather, after the good have toiled a little under them, he will free them from a harmful slavery that does not dare to come upon those who are ruled by God (Ps 124:3).

Solomon is inscribed on the song, because he built the temple (Ps 126:1-2). But it signifies the true Solomon, our Lord, the cause of the true and peaceful building. For this reason the building is shown to be made by God, and its guard is secure because it is guarded according to God. And this is fitting, because the buildings and guards made by human beings fell into vanity: the night watches of those who keep guard, and the diligent and laborious care by day. For this reason human things, being such as they are, came first, so that divine things alone might be recognized as having what is sure and unchangeable. Just as righteousness came through the law, so that God's righteousness might be seen after it as having what is genuine and alone true, and true life after the life that was in shadow and image.
"When he gives sleep to his beloved ones." He has indicated the rest from God that is like sleep and will be given out of love.

"For I have stretched you, Judah," he says, "for myself as a bow." Here too he calls the remaining saints the arrows of the Mighty One, for the defeat of the ungodly and those who are violent with injustice (Ps 126:4a).

The paths of entrance are many and various, and the lives of those who begin are of many kinds, but there is one perfection that reaches the height (Ps 127:1). He characterizes those who fear the Lord by saying next what sort of people they are: "Those who walk in his ways." For those who do not do this do not fear the Lord. The fear of the Lord is a turning away from evils, and the one who has turned away from evils is ready for the divine ways.

The cry "out of the depths" could mean out of the waters of afflictions that have poured around him. The endurance and the repetition of the same words belong to one who clings and hangs on and does not wish to let go of his supplication because of his desire (Ps 129:1b-2). For this reason he says, "Hear my voice, and let your ears be attentive."

The place did not become clear to David from the matter itself by his own forethought (Ps 131:6). For this reason he says, "We heard and we found," because a command of God pointed out the threshing floor of Ornan, on which he built the altar to turn away the death that was destroying the generation of the Hebrews (Ps 131:8). And having loved the discovery exceedingly, as one who had come to know what he had long desired, he rejoices in the matter and loves the worship there. There, he says, God also made a visitation, because the glory of God became manifest through the presence of the angel (Ps 131:9).
In the same way, he says, he foretells the time of Solomon, in which the ark is moved from the tent and set in the temple, and divine glory appeared and a cloud filled the house.
These things, he says, we see happened in Solomon's time according to David's words (Ps 131:10).

For the favor is toward David, even if the benefit extends to those after him (Ps 131:10). Just as it is said directly to Solomon that because of David he would not fall entirely from the kingdom, so also the sparing for David's sake passed to his descendants, just as it is said to Hezekiah: "I will shield this city for the sake of David my servant" (Ps 132:15).

For from the beginning he gave an abundance of food, which one translator calls "prey" and another renders as "grain." And he promises to make the inhabitants free from want. Concerning priests and holy ones he has made a decree that they be saved and attend to the sacred hymns. But when all these things had already been corrupted—the nation unable to enjoy the good things of the land because it had fallen under the power of the Romans, the priesthood failing, and all the joy in the temple dissolved—the great power arose there, the horn of David, which gores every power of enemies, a beautiful lamp shining with heavenly light for David and for his offspring, who, having begun there, sends out his radiance to the whole world, as the prophet Simeon says: "A light for revelation to the nations and for glory to your people Israel."

before: When the judge arrives, he says, many nations surround him, gathered together (Ps 7:8). He means the church, and he announces that the Lord says they will be gathered to him. When this happens, the judge will turn upward to the height, having handed over the kingdom.

The word uses winepress and harvest, as in the Gospel, to indicate the gathering of fruits at the consummation. The fruits are human works and thoughts, according to Isaiah, who says, 'I am coming to gather their works and their thoughts' (Isaiah 66:18) (Ps 8:1).

But, he says, you, the maker of such great works, care for a human being who is altogether small, and you remembered him when he fell away from you, and you looked after him when he was brought down into weakness (Ps 8:5). His creation was precious to you from the beginning, and he was made a little less than the angelic glory because of his earthly body. For glory surrounded him as one reigning over the works on earth that you had made, holding all irrational nature under himself—not only the land creatures, easily caught, but also the creatures of the air and the water. Each of these escapes human hands, the one by its movement in the height, the other by its hiding in the deep and its passage through the waters, but they are caught by wisdom and mind, and the earthly man captures the things in heaven and in the waters. From these things it is clear that in his intellectual nature he surpasses the irrational and mindless nature of animals, and he is comparable to the intellectual and angelic nature, while sharing with the irrational animals in his bodily nature.

He speaks of the manner of the new worship of God, the one without blood, and he shows the change that is in the Holy Spirit, according to which we are no longer what we were before, nor do we bear the same names—no longer children of men but children of God (Ps 15:4).
For having been heard before, he says, I ask to be heard now as well. For Paul says we pray with thanksgiving, because the remembrance of former things prepares the favors that follow (Ps 16:6).

He describes the work and the appearance of those who attack him. The work is murderous plotting and flattering words for an ambush. They are fattest in body, fenced about with fat, looking sideways with their eyes like a lion rushing to its prey and lying in wait secretly (Ps 16:10-12). Such was Saul toward David, saying that David had found favor in his eyes, ordering him to stand by, and keeping him as an attendant, yet attempting to kill him from ambush.

A hidden punishment has been prepared for them, he says, which will enter into their belly, according to what is said of Judas: 'May the curse enter like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones' (Psalm 108 [109]:18) (Ps 16:14c).

Again he sets apart love for God through love for the temple dedicated to him (Ps 26:4). For the one who loves God rejoices in the places dedicated to him, not enjoying his desire in the sight of these things—for it is a small thing to take pleasure in handmade works—but just as someone gladly looks at a garment or a book of the beloved, being stirred through these things to the memory of that person, so the God-loving person is stirred toward God through a house and a vessel dedicated to God (Ps 26:4). This one thing alone I have asked: to dwell in the temple of God, which Hannah does, and to rejoice in the beauty of the building as I look toward it. Now a house of God had not yet been built when David sang these things, but he brought the word up to the tabernacle and left it to those able to hear spiritually to raise the word up to the spiritual house (Ps 32:6).
In such passages the theology of the one God is made clear, encompassing the Trinity.

before: Having allegorized wandering, famine, thirst, darkness, and chains as the evils of the Jews, he now uses a maritime allegory as well. He brings the disturbances at sea, the changes from these into calm, and salvation even to a calm harbor into the same picture as their labors. And he shows that the rest which will succeed the labors came when their former calm was stirred into waves not without God, but by a divine command. It is as though the command raised a squall and stirred up with waves their former fair sailing. By these waves they are lifted up to a height as the waves crest, and brought down as the waves fall away, as tends to happen at sea: they are humbled, thrown into confusion, and bewildered to the point of losing their wits. Then they experience a change when the wind dies down, whenever God commands this too, and he releases the violence of the winds into a gentle breeze and quiets the sound of the waves. There they will have the joy that comes from the wilderness, and they will obtain the harbor they long for as a resting place. For these things it is fitting to give thanks to God, and in the church of the people and in the seat of the elders to sing hymns to him who handed the nation over to the waves because of sins, as has been said, but by mercy transferred them to good things. And the mercy itself shows that they had been brought forth from sins. For those who are shown mercy are not worthy of good things, but are pitiable because of their evils. This matter is not common in the way it often happens at sea, where the good are storm-tossed and shipwrecked, as Paul was, and the wicked are carried along by fair winds. The things that happen are common to both, so that when they are tested in the same circumstances they may reveal the difference in their disposition, which will later come to an upright and righteous recompense, witnessed beforehand by their very works. So the word is not about those who sail the sea, but about the people who are storm-tossed because of sin and will come to a harbor through mercy (Ps 108:21). For them there is a church of the people for confession and a seat of elders for the hymn of God.

The mercy he asks for is the mercy shown to human beings, on behalf of human beings. He is not himself in need of mercy, since he lightens the terrors of the worthy, being good in giving freely and not measuring out an equal return. But all things come to Christ, and he is shown mercy on our behalf. Insofar as he is us, he is pitied as poor and lowly. He is pitied as being in disturbances, insofar as he shared in the nature that is disturbed by evils. He is pitied as going into obscurity, insofar as his bodily manifestation was interrupted. He is pitied as one stirred up and lifted up like one of the lightest things, insofar as he handed himself over to those who seized him. He takes upon himself from us the weakness from fasting and the squalor from lack of washing, placing nothing between us and himself. And he calls the mockery from his enemies, which he now has through us who are reproached in his name, mockery upon these things.

He makes clear that the mighty authority of the divine king will be sent out over all the world, beginning from Jerusalem, according to the words: I was established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain (Psalm 2:6) (Ps 109:2). And all will obey and serve.

Apollinaris, setting beside it the rendering of Symmachus, says: The perpetual and unfading quality of his prime, proper to eternal life, is compared to morning dews, just as the life that was dissolved was compared to a shadow that declines (Ps 109:3). The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, and so on.

He is an eternal priest because he lives eternally, a priesthood made secure as if confirmed by an oath (Ps 109:4). Melchizedek is a type of him, whose death is not recorded as a sign that death does not even exist for him. Having just been shown as king, he is now also displayed as priest, which is impossible in Israel and under the law. And this too was prefigured in Melchizedek.

For it is clear that Christ was exalted even before the exaltation that came from human beings, since he was in the form of God and came down from heaven. Walking on the road and drinking water from a stream are symbols of lowliness. And we see the Lord traveling on foot and asking the Samaritan woman for water to drink.

In the present psalm the hymn is spoken in brief form, and the first sounds of the verses proceed through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrews according to the Hebrew language, from the first to the last, that is, from Aleph to Thau. Such a composition has grammatical elegance and invites one to a knowledge of letters and the learning of books. In this way the psalms immediately and clearly urge one to the study of the law, since Moses also commanded this from of old and ordered that they appoint teachers of letters and teach the law to children, because they had learning through hearing, not wisdom through the Spirit, as those who are perfected in Christ do (Ps 111:9).

before: The life to come is a living again, since we learn that the soul is not its own life, nor life in truth, if indeed the soul is not the human being. For if the soul possessed the truth of living in its life by itself, the dead thing would not have needed to live again. Therefore the Lord also said that the dead live for God, as not yet having life except insofar as it is in the power of God who gave them life. And he says that they have perished if they do not attain the resurrection, saying that he will raise up his own, so that the one from him may not be lost. And Paul likewise says, “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (1 Corinthians 15:18). To the sinner, godliness is a ridiculous character; but to the godly person, lawlessness is horrifying, because he foresees the terror of punishment (Ps 118:53).

“To me,” he says, “the only comfort is to look at your judgments, and my gladness is your commandments taken up in song and leading to joy through melody” (Ps 118:54). And I considered this the only good, as in a foreign and alien dwelling that can have no true good, because for the stranger the things at home are longed for, and before the return to them everything is painful.

God does not fashion a human being in the manner of a modeler, even though he is said to fashion, but such as a modeler would produce, he completes by the power that works such a shaping. And the present fashionings must be referred back to that first fashioning, as in “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) (Ps 118:73). So also Job says, “You fashioned me as clay” (Job 10:9), indicating the clay-fashioning in Adam upon himself. The request in the making is a thanksgiving, very fittingly the request for the intellectual power that makes the commandments understood. About this Paul also says, “Think about what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding in everything” (2 Timothy 2:7). The request is fitting as addressed to the Creator, as if to say: Care for your own workmanship, and perfect the living being that is intellectual by understanding. And what you prepared for your own kinship, make your own through your knowledge of your wishes. Since from the beginning the human being needed a command, by which his mind was set without need of many commands, and indeed having fallen away from that one, he needs more commands to fill the greater lack.

For without training in many evils and the help of God that comes beyond hope, a person cannot be firmly fixed in virtue. For those without contest are easily shaken when a struggle comes. Therefore, having recognized in himself the firmness that comes from many hardships, he hymns the confirming providence of God. Then he asks for rest from labors, saying, “Let your mercy come to comfort me, according to your word to your servant” (Ps 118:83).

Perhaps the righteous become dead rather than living under their afflictions, so as to resemble wineskins rather than human beings, losing their breath like settling frost, but choosing what is warm and active, as he says elsewhere, “They set me in dark places like the dead of the age” (Psalm 142 (143):3) (Ps 118:84). But even in such things, he says, I did not stand away from the God-taught righteousness, just as Joseph guarded his righteous self-control.
He calls promises commandments. Trusting, he says, in your promises and their truth, I seek help from you, my God (Ps 118:86).

He asks not to be handed over to the hands of those plotting against him unto death, asking for life—not yet the life eternal but the present one (Ps 118:88). And the death of the Savior is not only life, but also life-giving for human beings, becoming the release from death.

The resurrection, he says, will dissolve the conspiracy of the enemies against us and the betrayal of friends (Ps 40:10). This is what the heavenly voice testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

The permanence and eternal confirmation before God is that which is in heaven, which was also foretold in the fifteenth psalm after the resurrection in the words, “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15 [16]) (Ps 40:14). For he ascended into heaven to appear before the face of God on our behalf, bringing in himself what had been separated and alienated from the beginning (Ps 41:3).

From this the discerning person—whom the inscription summons—can understand that humanity came to be outside the face of God, so that through God it might seek restoration to the face of God. Rightly, then, does he seek the strong one, having fallen into weakness according to the words, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:2) (Ps 41:4). Hence it is necessary to have fallen into the present weakness. For not loving to endure by his own small strength, nor being able to do so, he seeks not to be left without true strength (Ps 41:4).

Those who have utterly forgotten the return to God, he says, consider the seeking of God to be vain and reproach those who do it. I was brought to tears, living with the most unpleasant grief instead of sweet food, according to what is said in Lamentations: “He fed me with ashes” (Lamentations 3:16). I did not abandon my desire because of the separation and the reproach, but I was grieved because righteousness was being reproached. Necessarily, then, the harassment of the wicked and the reproaches come, since the tears that come from these are not harmful to the righteous. For upon these rests the blessing: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). And immediately comes the comfort (Ps 41:6).

Do not let present things grieve you, he says, O soul, nor let them trouble you. But let hope in God console you, because we will obtain the good things worthy of thanksgiving and will have salvation at his appearing—which, according to Paul, is to await the appearing of the Lord and his kingdom. These things are intelligible concerning the future and the promises according to the law, and they reach higher, to what was said afterward by Paul [the text is corrupt here]: the better thing is to depart and be with Christ (Ps 41:7). What follows is a narrative of the things that still grieve.

Separation from the one desired melts the soul that desires. I am separated from God, he says as long as he does not yet see paradise, his own foundation from the beginning, but still dwells in the land of Jordan and Mount Hermon—very small compared to that one—and is troubled as if by storms of winds and crashing waves, with calamities rushing upon him one after another like torrents (Ps 41:9).

He teaches that the good things belong to the coming age, calling it the day in which God has promised to establish his mercy, according to what is said in Psalm 89: “Fill us in the morning with your mercy” (Psalm 89:14 [90:14]) (Ps 41:10). But the present time, he says, is for gladness, when it is night and darkness, the conversation with God through hymns and the stretching out in prayer.

before: Every remedy and help brought to them through their own kind had failed against their incurable diseases. So after all those things, the Savior came, as was fitting, healing every disease and every sickness, so as to remove even their deadness and death. For this truth, then, the Savior shone forth in the time of Augustus, when the time had been fulfilled, since the salvation of human beings was being accomplished suitably (Ps 102). About this the present word also says: "For it is time to have mercy on Zion, O Master, and you, having risen up through yourself, will have mercy on her" (the title of Psalm 102 [103]).

A thanksgiving had to follow the preceding prophecy. This has also been arranged through this song: the mercy of God and the judicial righteousness are glorified, because through mercy he will rescue the people from those who wrong them, and there is the removal of corruption, and the grace kept for successors, and the heavenly kingdom that will pass over all things.
The heaven is not a sphere encircling the whole and running around it, but it roofs the earth, stretched around it, being roofed from above by waters with a stable and fixed standing (Ps 103).

It is clear that "stretching out" and "roofing" and "making" stand for "having stretched out" and "having roofed" and "having made." So also "forming the spirit of a human being within him": since the formation by God happened once for all, earth and the finished products from it come to be continually, according to which it is also said: "My Father is working until now, and I am working" (John 5:17). And "I am the one who is" (Exodus 3:14) would also contribute to this, since created things do not exist but come to be, having a generated nature, and for this reason their substance is understood in their coming to be and does not truly exist as the maker does. And this extends through the holy Trinity, which is creative.

He speaks of the wonder of the foundation as a proof of God's power: that the earth, being the heaviest element, has been fixed above the waters and remains unmoved forever, since the abyss beneath it can neither support nor establish it, but covers it like garments, so that its seat is ineffable and belongs to God's power, not to the nature of the elements (Ps 103).

The earth gives springs of water that gush up from the beginning, and these too by God's power; and he says that they often dry up and go into hiding by the fear of God, which is said more clearly in Psalm 73 (74):15: "You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up other rivers" (Ps 103). He also marvels at the position of the mountains, raised up unmoved above the plains and not dragged down by the appointed force to cover what lies beneath, according to: "They will say to the mountains, 'Cover us'" (Hosea 10:8) (Ps 103:13).

He calls the air the upper rooms of God, as if the whole world were one house. And he says the rain is the work of the Son, from which the earth receives its fruitfulness (Ps 103:17). And he would be saying that the drawing up of the waters from the sea is his work (Ps 103:17b).
And about the heron it is also said through Jeremiah: "Even the heron in the sky knows its times" (Jeremiah 8:7) (Ps 103:26b).

God is said to mock him, that is, to count his cunning as nothing. For God laughs at everyone who opposes him because of its futility, and counts it as play because of how easily it is caught, as he says about the Egyptians: "How many things I have mocked against the Egyptians" (Exodus 10:2) (Ps 103:27-28).

Others have taken the preceding words about the food supplied to living creatures. For when this is present, it flourishes and rejoices; when it is absent, it is pressed by want and thrown into confusion by the lack of necessities (Ps 103:29-30).

This is the work of Christ, who also says that he is the resurrection and the life, and has promised to raise all, and when he was present, he gave life to those he wished (Ps 103:31). So what is said belongs to the Father as the source, to the Son as the worker, and to the Spirit as the one who is participated in and, as it were, brought in through the Son into the life of all things, according to: "He will give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you" (Romans 8:11). The Spirit, then, is life-giving through the life it works, and deifying through the participation it grants; and the human spirit is named after it, according to its formation by it (Ps 103:32).
Eternal is the glory of the one who keeps his works forever; and since the glory is eternal, the things that glorify are eternal (Ps 103:33).

The greatness of the glory is shown by the fear of creation, and the fear reveals the subjection. Thus the psalm says that the sea was subjected by being afraid (Ps 103:34). For what fears is subjected; and the subjection of the earth is the trembling at the oversight of God, and the smoking of the mountains is like burning, which was also seen bodily happening on Mount Sinai (Ps 103:33-34).

He speaks of the wonder of the foundation as a proof of God's power: that the earth, being the heaviest element, has been fixed above the waters and remains unmoved forever, since the abyss beneath it can neither support nor establish it, but covers it like garments, so that its seat is ineffable and belongs to God's power, not to the nature of the elements (Psalm 104:5-6).

He calls the air the upper rooms of God, as if the whole world were one house. And he says the rain is the work of the Son, from which the earth receives its fruitfulness (Psalm 104:13). And he would be saying that the drawing up of the waters from the sea is his work (Psalm 104:13).

God is said to mock him, that is, to count his cunning as nothing. before: Then God is spoken of in divine terms as the Creator, and the creation is the work of the Word and the Spirit. It is clear that the words are human, since a mouth is mentioned from which word and spirit come, but they are understood differently when applied to God, according to his uncompounded and entirely bodiless nature. That is, the Word exists with God who exists, and the Spirit exists. The Word is the manifestation of the Father, and for this reason he is named Word. The Spirit is the participation in the Word, as Spirit from the mouth. When he says heavens and powers of the heavens, he does not divide the creation, assigning the heavens to the Word and the powers to the Spirit, for the works of the Trinity are undivided. Rather, he expresses the same thing in different ways. As in the verse, Jacob entered into Egypt and Israel sojourned in the land of Ham, the entrance does not refer to one person, Jacob, and the dwelling to another, Israel. The parallel expresses the same thing, and we would find this custom in many places.

On Psalm 33:7 (34:7). David, showing himself, says that he became poor, that he was in anguish in his flight, and that he escaped this danger by the will of God, since the scheme of madness would not otherwise have prevailed if not for God's will (Ps 33:7).

On Psalm 33:9 (34:9). He uses taste metaphorically for the experience of things, which was present to him at that time (Ps 33:9). What happened to him through God's goodness, that he was not overlooked while being pursued by a foreign king but was saved from two most severe and powerful enemies, this he sets before all in common, as something that did not happen only to him but would also happen to others, as many as join themselves to God through hope in God. Blessedness must consist in this, and in nothing else, as David says in the verse, Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.

On Psalm 33:20 (34:20). He commands us to look to the end and to take courage in the release from afflictions, not to be distressed at the beginning itself whenever affliction happens to occur (Ps 33:20). For the soul must be prepared in this way, not as one that will not suffer, but as one that will not be defeated by its sufferings.

On Psalm 34:1-3 (35:1-3). He shapes the speech about God into complete likeness of a human being, as Isaiah also does, in order to show that what is impossible in him is possible for God, asking him to wage war and to be armed with shield and spear and to shut off the attacks of enemies with a middle wall. Isaiah also shows this in Christ, foreseeing him coming from the punishment of the unjust with his garment reddened from the slaughter of the foreigners: Who is this who has come from Edom, redness of garments from Bozrah, and the rest? (Isaiah 63:1). So the things that are referred to the Father in divine terms clearly belong to the Son and are fulfilled in the Son.

On Psalm 34:5 (35:5). That they become invisible is turned against them, like dust driven by the wind. They are driven out not by a human hand, for the righteous suffer this rather at the hands of the unjust, but this happens through angels, as the Lord says: The holy ones will go out and will choose the unjust from the midst of the righteous and will separate them (Matthew 13:49). For now the discordant elements are mixed together, but then they will be divided according to the difference of their manner, according to what was said again by the Savior: And many dwelling places are with my Father (John 14:2).

On Psalm 34:6 (35:6). The ways of the impious, he says, are dark; they do not know how they advance (Ps 34:6). He asks that this be accomplished, praying that the deed of the unjust be held in darkness, since it belongs to darkness, and that they fall after slipping, because they walk a slippery road, for nothing in injustice has firmness, and that they become invisible, pursued by angels, which is what they themselves do against the righteous (Ps 34:13).

On Psalm 34:13 (35:13). He flees, he says, to his own strength, which is God. For a person seeks God with fastings and humiliations, turning the whole soul to invocations of God through freedom from bodily pleasures, when the invocations linger in the mind during prayer and slip into the bosom of the soul.

On Psalm 35:6 (36:6). For the things ordered by God are firm and unshaken, such as what was said to Noah, that he would no longer bring a flood for the destruction of living creatures, which agrees with the word about God's forbearance (Ps 35:6). before: But these hopes, he says, are firm and unshakable, and we will not abandon them because of what has happened. Yet what has happened now is the opposite of them. For we have been left behind by you, he says, having been thrust away, and you are not present with our armies. The shame that then seized the battles has come around upon us, and we have been diminished before those whom we formerly mastered, and we have been plundered by those whom we plundered. For in this it has been shown all the more by God that the strength belonged to Israel, since when they are abandoned they are defeated—just as for man, being abandoned became the occasion of death, showing that resurrection comes from God alone and in no other way (Ps 43:12).

We have been gripped by cowardice, he says, a cowardice unable to defend us against those who devour us like sheep. This is the cowardice that Moses also threatened would seize them for their transgressions, because the sound of a driven leaf would pursue them. And we have become captives, he says, and we have been scattered among the nations—we who were formerly brought out from the nations and possessed the holy land. This is a dissolution of honor, just as for man the dissolution of his formation is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). So also Isaiah says about the people: “We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your mercy was not called upon us” (Isaiah 63:19) (Ps 43:13a).

Freely they were sold, as Isaiah also says. And he says they were sold for their sins, just as Paul says about man: “I am fleshly, sold under sin” (Romans 7:14). The sale is the alienation and the coming to be under human masters instead of God. This is what he also threatened Jeroboam and the people with him through Shemaiah the prophet: that they would become slaves to the Egyptian king Shishak, and they would know the slavery of God and the slavery of the kings of the earth (Ps 43:15).

For such a thing is a parable—that they are remembered in the curses. Just as Jeremiah says against the false prophets: “They will take up a curse against him in the exile, O Judah, in Babylon, saying, ‘May the Lord do to you as he did to Zedekiah and as to Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in fire because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel’” . Grant these things now, and most justly: they are devoured like sheep, when they led Christ like a sheep to slaughter; they are sold to the nations, just as they bought the Lord, betrayed for silver and in some way handed over to death; they are mocked, just as they made mockery and shaking of heads at the crucified Lord (Ps 43:18-21).

This alone remains to Israel as a hope for the recall of those who are left, which the prophecy foreseeing says: that they did not turn aside to the customs of the Greeks according to the idolatry they had agreed upon, nor did they swerve from the path of piety toward the one God that had been commanded them, even though they were so humbled and exiled and placed under the authority of those who kill. This was preserved especially by those around Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who endured fire rather than accept worship of idols. And indeed, this is not present as something pious among the remaining Jews at the present time. For while they do not entirely abandon the practice of not going to idols or the Greek sickness of incantations, their impiety toward Christ is shown to be most harmful in this way: because, not worshiping idols as before, they are enslaved as never before (Ps 44:2).

For he has come as the fulfiller of what is not truly fulfilled among human beings, lawful by divine purity and by the sanctifying participation that comes from him. And he indicates that he will say many things quickly, comparing the tongue that declares these things to the pen of a very swift scribe.

Isaiah foresees his outward appearance failing compared to the sons of men, prophesying his dishonor according to the flesh (Ps 44:3ab). But David interprets the divine beauty, which is also made clear in Isaiah through the words that the king will be seen with glory.

He appears to be seeking something greater and beyond human capacity, belittling the life we now live as being nothing (Ps 88:49). He says that human beings pass into something vain—not that they came into being for vanity—and he asks that they not be handed over to corruption, since clearly the kingdom will also be restored then, when corruption is dissolved and life for the ages is given. No one exists who will live and not die, nor will anyone be able to rescue himself from death. These words plainly seek the heavenly king, the redeemer from vanity, the one who is stronger than death and the Savior of human beings from death, who changes the vanity of the present life into truth and establishes an eternal kingdom upon eternal life.

He did not despair of mercy, but he seeks the promise and calls upon the righteousness of God against the impious nations who reproach the righteous man for having suffered misfortune in his offspring and having fallen (Ps 88:51). He says these are enemies of God, and they reproach the footprint of the righteous king as if it had been wiped out. After making these appeals, he blesses. The blessing belongs to one who hopes. And what does he hope for, except that the prayers will be fulfilled, that the promise will be accomplished and not fail, as he appears to have believed from the beginning? As Paul also says, "It is not as though the word of God has failed" (cf. Romans 9:6).
If he has spoken this way about a thousand years, it is clear that the span of a human life will be the thinnest possible, as if indivisible (Ps 89:10).

The whole of human life, he says, is bounded by about seventy years. He says this from the greater part. And not even this is given in ease, but almost entirely in hardship. For either we are disciplined as infants, or we labor as young men, or we suffer hardship as old men. So he rightly said, "And the greater part of them is labor and pain" (Psalm 89:10 (90:10)) (Ps 89:17). For since the order of life follows age in this way, very little time is found that is stolen away for gladness.

He fittingly called this entire time "night," in which a human being sleeps while being put to death, and "morning" the time that is coming, in which we will live when the Lord appears and mercy comes down from heaven. He asks that the sun come and the day shine forth, and that enduring gladness be given to the righteous in place of the days in which we were afflicted, falling into countless evils. Next he says that a thousand will fall on the left and ten thousand on the right, before they can even draw near and inflict any harm, so that he will look without fear, by the recompense from God, upon those falling and being destroyed (Ps 90:8). For it says, "They came to the watchtower of the wilderness and looked and saw the multitude, and behold, all were dead, fallen on the ground, and there was no one saved" (2 Chronicles 20:24). But one must not always suppose that victories come to the righteous without battle. For they often won by going through battle as well, but he speaks here of the most manifest help, in which God the helper is especially seen (Ps 90:9).

He introduced the person of the one who hopes, saying from himself to God that he has made him his hope. And again he declares to such a person: "Since you have chosen the Most High like a house of security, you will be mastered by no evil, nor will your house be struck by divinely sent blows" (Ps 90:10).

before: Continuing with the words of the comparison, he says, "I have become like those who have been slain and lie in a tomb" (Psalm 87:6 (88:5)). For he bore everything that is heavy and afflicting to a body. For instead of "My eyes have grown weak from poverty" (Psalm 87:10 (88:9)), Symmachus rendered, "My eye has poured out from affliction."

Save, then, the race you have made, by your own knowledge, and lead back to life the human beings who have fallen into death in each way (Ps 87:13). They must be spectators of your wonders and interpreters of your power. Let them not remain overlooked in forgetfulness, but let them be remembered again by you and led back to life. This is what the champion of human beings says, interceding for the common race of all and working out the life of the world by the will of the Father.

The ambassador and priest presents himself on our behalf with unceasing presentation, from dawn and through the night, and he appeases the wrath of God against us, which he himself took upon himself in his sufferings (Ps 87:14).

He calls "exaltation" the exaltation in wonders and signs, about which the Father says to him, "I have glorified it" (John 12:28), while the Son says, "Glorify your Son" (John 17:1) (Ps 87:16). He says this was changed into humiliation when he came to suffer, suffering for human beings and abandoned by them, the ones for whom he suffered.

Mount Tabor lies in the region of the Galileans, and Hermon in the desert near Sinai (Ps 88:13). God must be hymned, he says, not only for his works around Tabor but also for the manifestation that took place around Hermon.

"Your power," he says, "prevails" (Ps 88:14-15). Let your strength appear, let it become manifest and glorious among human beings. All these things he has included as spoken to one God. We know his power as one and only, and his arm and hand as perfect. Through it all things have come into being and are coming into being, so that it, being perfect in itself, is numbered with God according to the one number of divinity, and in no way falls into what is said about the many sons, none of whom the word has said beforehand is like the true one. For the one true power is not like that, but is uniquely the true image and mark of God, God accomplishing all things through it. Therefore the divine things were fitted to its sojourn among human beings, and the judgment of God is dispensed by Christ. This power exists as the power of God, but was given as to a human being, as Christ himself said, and God divided mercy and judgment by the times. He foretold the judgment from then on, when the king comes and sits on the throne of his glory. For that throne has righteousness as its foundation, as Aquila also said beforehand in the ninth psalm: "He set his throne in judgment" (Psalm 9:8 (9:7)). Before that manifestation, mercy was abundant on the earth, like a forerunner of the critical coming, as the fearful judge who is about to appear prepares human beings for salvation by mercy. And with mercy comes truth, because it is not possible for anything untrue or not upright to occur in God's good patience, even if it seems to those who do not know the future that the wicked are wrongly allowed to prosper, nor is it reasonable that the good are overlooked when they suffer loss.

He now explicitly recounts the promise made through Nathan the prophet, indicating prophets in the plural from one, whom he also calls sons of God, or as the other interpreters render it, holy ones of God (Ps 88:20-25).

before: The unjust are blind to the beauty of righteousness and do not see clearly the dignity and grace of the words about it. But the one who has chosen these words and wished to belong to them—this person alone is established in understanding, because wisdom reveals her own beauty only to her lovers, as it is written: “Love her, and she will honor you; honor her, that she may embrace you” (Proverbs 4:6, 8).

All good things in a person come through practice, and so he was extended along with the intensity of his practice, so that through it he surpassed the elder, the young man, and the disciple—surpassing his teachers.
Presenting himself as humble and obedient, he asks for the salvation that comes from this, from God who gives grace to the humble and has promised mercy to those who love him (Ps 118:107).

It is a greater proof of eagerness to pass through dangers and not stand away from the law, and to be in the midst of plots and not be dragged away from righteous things by anger and irritation toward those plotting against him (Ps 118:109-110). Thus Saul’s plot did not lead David astray into avenging himself, even where that might have seemed fitting.

He intensified the demonstration of his zeal for the law when he said he had set the law as his own inheritance, choosing to live in it not for a time but forever, not as under a yoke of necessity but holily in gladness of soul. For what is done with gladness is lasting and hard to overturn.

Even if they are not hateful insofar as they are human, it is not unworthy of God that such people are said to be hateful to God, according to the words: “You hated all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 5:6 (5:5)) (Ps 118:113). For this reason Jehoshaphat’s friendship with such a person became a reproach through the prophet, because he loved the one hated by God (Ps 118:118-119).

He shows an imitation of God. If every apostate from the ordinances is made worthless by God for his vain thoughts, then to him also they appear no more valuable than grape-pressings or dross. Therefore he is stirred up to love of the divine commands, taking the vanity of the wicked as an encouragement to care for what is good. The fifth edition reads: “They were counted as nothing.”

He longs for what is lacking to be filled up by God’s forbearance, since God waits for the good work that is still to come, as if guaranteeing that it will be fulfilled—just as those who guarantee debtors do so to keep them from falling badly into deceptions (Ps 118:122). He asks for this because precision about sound teaching is difficult amid disturbances and griefs (Ps 118:134).

before: Symmachus rendered it, “And they will fear him as long as the sun endures” (Ps 72:5), in agreement with what Gabriel said to the holy virgin: “The Lord will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Psalm 71 [72]) (Ps 71:10-11).

Here, then, David’s prayers are fulfilled—the prayers he made for the eternal permanence of the throne when he said: “Lord, the word you spoke concerning the house of your servant and concerning your servant, let it be made faithful forever; and do as you have spoken, and let your name be exalted forever, while they say, ‘The Lord Almighty is the God of Israel,’ and the house of David your servant is raised up.” Unreasonably, then, was the heading written on the next psalm: “The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended.” For this psalm is the end of that collection, and part of the thanksgiving for the fulfillment of David’s prayers.

The second book of psalms also ended with a blessing that sounds out the “Amen,” just as the first book’s “May it be” makes clear, as has been said. For the end of that first book was Psalm 40, spoken in reference to Christ, and the end of this second book is the one just mentioned, Psalm 71. The third book ends—so that I may speak about it now as well—at Psalm 88, so that there are in all 17 psalms, of which 11 are by Asaph, then 4 by the sons of Korah, 1 by David, and Heman the Israelite’s is last.

Instead of “They passed through into the disposition of the heart,” Aquila rendered, “They passed by the watchtowers of the heart.” This means they are unwilling to carry out any of their natural thoughts, nor do they practice what they understand to be good, but they turn away from these things. Virtue is a joke to them; slander against their inferiors comes easily; blasphemy against God is ready at hand; their tongue is quick against human beings. And this is what “their tongue passed through upon the earth” means (Ps 72:11, 13).

The righteous [will be blessed] in the future state, as Jeremiah also says something of this kind: “If you turn back, I will restore you before my face” (Jeremiah 15:19). There he says, “And all who planned evil, who chose evil, will change their minds.” For when the good things appear among the race of the righteous, they will say, “There is, then, a providence of God; and how does he know what is done?” This is the voice of those who have lost their natural reasoning because of the good things that came to them unprofitably, leading them into injustices. For prospering contrary to reason produces thoughts that the world is not governed according to reason, nor will he know our [the text is damaged here; perhaps: hardships]. But although providence stands over all things, nevertheless, he says, these impious people, who are unbearable in their arrogance and in their words against God even amid their good cheer, and who are not yet persuaded by the approval of the righteous—they mock [the text is damaged here] the one who is steadfast of hands [perhaps: clean of hands, as in Psalm 72:13] as a vain steadfastness, and they speak evil of the one who chooses righteousness. This is the difficulty of human reasoning: to repent of zeal for virtue as though it were not good or profitable. Such thoughts often enter many people’s minds, and he intends to heal them by his word. To destroy the impious reasoning, he confirms the more pious reasoning through the person of God. For what is said truly requires God as guarantor: that the pious who now suffer hardship are more blessed in the future state than the impious who prosper to the end. Such is the saying in Jeremiah: “If you turn back, I will restore you before my face” (Jeremiah 15:19). And “They said, ‘How does God know?’” is the voice of those who have lost their natural reasoning through unprofitable luxury; for if providence exists, they would not prosper while the good suffer hardship (Ps 72:24).

But since this was not in us, nor was it possible among human beings to be holy by nature, but there is need of gift and heavenly grace, for this reason the Spirit came upon Christ, so that he might show us as led from him to participation in the Spirit through kinship according to the body (Ps 44:12a).

before: This carries a threat of retributions, because it is impossible for anything to happen contrary to what is just when righteousness is the overseer of what takes place. So even those who now escape the punishing retributions, or who do not receive their retributions, will certainly receive them later. And this is unchangeable with God, as Paul said with confidence that God, the righteous judge, will give him the crown of righteousness on that day (2 Timothy 4:8) (Ps 35:10a).
On Psalm 35:10a (36:9a). The things that lead to life are supplied abundantly by God, and if they were not supplied, life would be destroyed (Ps 35:10b).

On Psalm 35:10b (36:9b). He is illuminated, he says, by the light from heaven, by the one who set the sun as the light of day. But these things are common to the righteous and the unrighteous, and in them he marveled at God's philanthropy, since the ungrateful are not excluded from enjoying what comes from God. But what is exceptional and proper to God's own is something else.

On Psalm 36:7 (37:7). He commands to be still and wait for God, not being disturbed by present things but hoping for future things, according to the apostolic word: Rejoicing in hope, enduring in affliction (Romans 12:12), and Jeremiah's word: It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth (Ps 36:7). He will sit alone and be silent; he will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches.

On Psalm 36:9 (37:9). He commands us to look far off and not be astounded by present things, and to foresee the destruction of the wicked and the preservation of the good (Ps 36:12). These things clearly reach their end in another age, since the present age does not have the outcomes of these things, but rather the wicked prevail over the things on earth. Therefore he says, The whole world lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19).

On Psalm 36:14ab (37:14ab). He says that the wicked set in motion against themselves the very things they prepare against the righteous, as if someone drew a sword and was slain by it, and the plot too will be futile, like a bow shattered in the hand of an archer (Ps 36:13). In David's case this was also fulfilled bodily: David struck with their own sword, the one they had drawn against David (cf (Ps 36:17). 1 Samuel 17:51).

On Psalm 36:27 (37:27). Such an exhortation again comes from the prediction: to flee from evil and practice the doing of good in hope of eternal rest, and the reasoning about the matter is that the overseer is righteous and does not overlook his own.

On Psalm 37:4a (38:4a). He compares his great suffering and many afflictions to a body entirely afflicted, as in Isaiah: From the soles of the feet to the head there is no soundness in it, but wounds and bruises, the burning inflammation of a threat (Isaiah 1:6) (Ps 37:4). These are signs of wrath, and the cause of the wrath is sins, so that the sufferings bring awareness of sins, and in this way they benefit souls, just as bodies are brought from insensibility to sensation (Ps 37:12).

On Psalm 37:12 (38:12). He laments the desertion of friends and the uprising of enemies, which are also seen in the Savior's sufferings, when the disciples were scattered in fear, and the wicked used every bitterness and malice against him, toward whom he also fulfilled the silence predicted here.

On Psalm 37:14 (38:14). Having, he says, just grounds to answer those who slandered him, but knowing that speech would not be for their benefit, I bore the false accusations without resentment (Ps 37:14). And as one who does not hear, I was silent, and as one who has no reproof. For what would I say and answer? It was for nothing, as the Lord also said: If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask you, you will not answer (Luke 22:67-68). When people do not listen, speech is useless toward them, but useful toward God who hears.

On Psalm 37:22-23 (38:22-23). Human beings would not say these things about themselves, but Christ, in place of human beings and for human beings, suffering as a righteous one at the hands of the unrighteous and taking what is theirs upon himself, would say them: in one place, Why have you forsaken me? (Ps 37:22) in another, Do not forsake me, and Do not depart from me, since this is impossible for him (Ps 37:23). For I am not alone, he says, because my Father is with me. He asks for the salvation of human beings as his own, having something proper to the request as far as the human element in the mixture with divinity is concerned—this was the passible element naturally united to the flesh—and also having the dignity of the nature that transcends, by which he fulfilled the things of the request.

On Psalm 38:4 (39:4). And hearing, he says, and reckoning up the bold and abusive words of the enemy, and seeing how great an authority of speech he used, to whom it was not fitting even to speak, I was kindled with indignation on behalf of the righteousness that was being dishonored (Ps 38:4).

On Psalm 38:8a (39:8a). I do not, he says, have anything in myself worthy of expectation, but I wait, expecting what is with you and what is yours, enduring in present labors in hope of future good things (Ps 38:8).

On Psalm 38:9b (39:9b). I bear, he says, being reproached now and not answering back, knowing in some such way that God wills me to be trained by reproaches (Ps 38:9). So David himself bore being reviled by Shimei, saying that the Lord had told him to curse David (2 Samuel 16:10).

before: So the arrangement of these songs followed the same order. After the prayer for Israel came thanksgiving, and hymns were proclaimed beforehand, and acts of worship toward God. For by his mercy and truth, because of the glory of the word of God above every name of his—that is, what has now been accomplished—God is glorified in the name of the Word as he was never glorified before. Before the manifestation of the Word, the worship of God occupied only a portion of the earth. He was hymned as maker of all things, and he was proclaimed as the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, but all of this had its knowledge and honor only as far as the Hebrew nation. But when his living oracle appeared, coming forth from God and revealed to the world through a body, then every nation and the whole inhabited world runs together to the worship of God, serves the name of the Word, and glorifies God in the presence of the Word. Now worship has increased among the nations according to mercy, and it is preserved for Israel according to the truth of the promises.

Psalm 137 (138):3. He shows the great favor and the swift obedience, and the supply of power given to souls in the name of Christ (Ps 137:3). For Christ says, "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:13). And the apostle says that the supply of the Spirit comes to those who believe.

Psalm 137 (138):5. Let the providence of God be hymned, because God is great and his greatness is revealed through providence. Just as through the seraphim the glory of God in his present providence and economy was hymned when they cried out, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory" (Isaiah 6:3) (Ps 137:5; Ps 137:6).

Psalm 137 (138):6. Because, he says, the human creation enjoys the gift of God, and the lesser and formerly more dishonored part of it—the nations—is not now overlooked either. Since all things are small before God, it is no wonder if he extends his benefits even to the smallest—that is, to those who had no hope and were without God in the world, whom the apostle calls "those who are not" (Ps 137:7-8a).

Psalm 137 (138):7–8a. He brings in the second part, the portion of Israel, which has been caught up in afflictions but will be restored to salvation. For he will repay on behalf of the wronged nation, so as to rescue them from the hands of those who oppress them (Ps 137:8c).
Psalm 137 (138):8c. Even if, he says, we do not produce fruits worthy of your love, yet because we are your works, we ask not to be overlooked (Ps 137:8c).

before: He asks for understanding, he says, and promises that it will not be without fruit. For I will not only learn, he says, but I will also keep your statutes (Psalm 118:7-8, 119:7-8) (Ps 118:10).

Aquila says, “Do not let me go astray in ignorance.” Using his desire for the law, he fears the lack of understanding that turns many people’s zeal to the opposite. Even in what they think they are doing rightly, they have stumbled, as Solomon says: “There is a way that seems right to people, but its end goes down to the bottom of Hades” (Proverbs 14:12).
For understanding does not come immediately from memory but from divine illumination. The statutes are the things that can make righteous (Psalm 118:12, 119:12).

Pride is the mother of lawlessness. Because of it they refuse to obey God’s commands, like the disobedient people who say, “We shall not be mastered, and we will not come to you any longer.” He says this to show his own eagerness before God for obedience to the commandments. Because God understands them to be guilty, he will rebuke those who are disobedient and unsubmissive through pride (Psalm 118:21, 119:21).

He prays to escape true dishonor in the sight of God, which the Lord shows to be most fearful, saying that those who put him to shame will be put to shame (Ps 118:22). Showing the opposite of this, this man of the law says here that though he is mocked by great and proud people, he does not turn away from the study of the sacred oracles and from correction by them (Ps 118:23). And a little later he says, “I spoke of your testimonies before kings and was not ashamed” (Psalm 118:22-23, 119:22-23). Such is Paul when he says, “For I am not ashamed of the gospel” (Romans 1:16).

What he himself says is a sacrifice to God—a broken and humbled heart—he now says he has fulfilled by bringing his soul down as if to the ground and humbling himself willingly (Ps 43:25). About the unwilling humiliation he says, “Our soul was humbled to the dust; our belly clung to the earth” (Psalm 43:26 (44:25)). So having brought himself forward as humbled as is fitting, he seeks from God as recompense a lawful way of life and life according to God’s word. And this very thing is also a mark of humility: not to place the good life in one’s own power but to seek it from God (Psalm 118:25, 119:25).

It is a great thing to do everything as in the sight of God, and to say these things and recount them, and to ask for revelation about them that corrects or confirms (Ps 118:26-27). And he will also gain benefit for others by speaking from more divine understanding and proclaiming the wonderful kindness of God that is stored up for those who act in holiness. For the one who teaches about righteousness also teaches about its end, which is stored up for it—something wonderful and unexpected, because God rewards greatly and beyond what is deserved. Paul also spoke about self-control and righteousness and the coming judgment, so that the governor became afraid (Acts 24:25). Instead of “I will meditate,” Aquila says “I will converse,” and Symmachus says “I will explain” (Psalm 118:26-27, 119:26-27).

He uses the order of the plagues indifferently and does not list them all, because, I think, the power of God is shown even from the wonders that are mentioned one by one (Ps 104:15). What is needed is that God's power be made known, not that a complete record of events be produced. He says the frogs were not simply produced on the earth, but in the houses, and in the most prominent parts of the houses, and in their innermost rooms, so that their onslaught was unhindered and most violent, and no one, not even the most powerful, could stop them (Ps 104:27). It was also extraordinary that the gnats and the dog-fly were poured out over the whole land and stopped at the borders without going further, so that the punishment was clearly being carried out against Egypt alone. That is why the turning of the waters to blood also stopped at the borders, and the streams flowing into the neighboring country were no longer such, because the punishment was against the Egyptians, taking away the abundance of the river (Ps 104:37).

Along with the salvation that was given, he also speaks of the abundance that came from God's power, which led the Egyptians to provide many costly things to those who asked and were about to leave the country (Ps 105:14). It was also a great thing that they departed unharmed, every one of them, from a country that was suffering the worst plagues.

When they tested God in the waterless place, he, who cannot be tempted and bears no grudge, did not repay them, but gave them their request. And when they provoked him bitterly as they went up at the Red Sea, even then he made known to them his power. But when they angered Moses and Aaron in the camp, then the earth opened and swallowed them. For the servants were not to be despised. But since kindness and severity are both with him, according to the words, See then the kindness and the severity of God, he first gave them the things of kindness. And when they did not benefit from it, he accordingly treated them with the fitting medicine of punishment. So the followers of Dathan and Abiram angered Moses by saying, Has God spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us as well? (Numbers 12:2). And Korah and his company, who dared to bring strange fire and offer sacrifices to God in the place of the priests, angered Aaron. But those who spoke against Moses—Dathan with his whole family—the earth opened wide and swallowed, and it covered the company of Abiram. And Korah and those with him who were about to offer their censers, a flame came out from the tabernacle and consumed them.

According to justice, the decree was destruction; according to love for humanity, there was the concession of being saved. The intercession made room for the concession, both because of the holiness of the one interceding and because of the providence over the world by which the intercessor pleaded, so that the grace of God toward Israel might not be thought incomplete, and because of the memory of the fathers and the promise made to them, which Moses recalled as he pleaded. For according to their impiety and the foreknowledge of their whole wickedness, they would have been destroyed.

The dispute about the land was older than the rebellion of Korah and Dathan, but greater and more impious, since it fought against the promise of God and was not striving about the worship of God. So it is fittingly joined with the impiety toward God mentioned before, since it came about through cowardice just as that one came about through faintheartedness. Cowardice produces despair of success, just as faintheartedness, because of Moses' separation, produced despair of Moses' return.

before: The words of supplication are also spoken in songs. But since supplication must be offered with thanksgiving, the song is placed before the prayer. For no one who has been ungrateful for what came before is strong in asking for what is to come. And the request seeks divine remembrance from God. For if I were in remembrance with you, the psalmist says, I would not be going about in gloom and being oppressed by the unjust.
